name: Kingdom of Aksum (Ezana)

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes Axum II (350-599) at 600,000-700,000 km2 and Axum I (to 349) at 300,000-400,000 (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/208, low). High 1.25 million km2 for 350 is Turchin, Adams and Hall (2006) in the infobox of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Aksum, which counts the claimed Nubian and Arabian lands. The world_300 Axum polygon measures only 89,000 km2 (the Tigray and Eritrean highland core), so the map understates the realm.

population.note: Seshat codes Axum II (350-599) at 500,000-600,000 and its Axum I page quotes "at the outside half a million" for the kingdom without its Arabian and Nubian territories (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/208). High: HYDE via OWID (https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/population) has Ethiopia 861,709 (300) and 1,053,627 (400) and Eritrea 36,036-38,808, about 1.0 million for both modern countries in 350, a ceiling since the kingdom held only the north.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Aksum covered 80-100 ha in the first four centuries CE, 4,500 to 20,000 people at 50-200 per ha (Seshat https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/208); Seshat codes its largest settlement at 50,000-60,000 for 350-599 (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/210, high). Adulis, Matara and Qohaito were smaller towns.

activePersonnel.note: Educated guess. No army size survives. The inscriptions name royal armies (sarawit) sent out as separate columns, and the RIE 186 passage on the road Ousanas built for tribute and troop provisions names four sarawit (Hatke 2013, pp. 32-34). RIE 189, Ezana's Nubian campaign of c. 360, tallies 602 men and 156 women and children killed, 629 prisoners, 10,560 cattle and 51,050 sheep; an earlier campaign resettled some 4,400 Beja (Hatke 2013, Aksum and Nubia, pp. 124-130, https://dlib.nyu.edu/awdl/isaw/hatke2013-aksum-and-nubia/). Tallies of that order fit field armies of a few thousand to about 10,000.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Clan levies of free men called out for campaigns; see mobilizationRatio.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Boat crews at Adulis, commissariat and the officials who tallied spoils.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. Clan levies: De Blois (via Hatke 2013 n. 484, https://dlib.nyu.edu/awdl/isaw/hatke2013-aksum-and-nubia/) reads Ge'ez hara "troops" as making every free clansman a soldier, so a larger share than a salaried empire.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Educated guess. Spearmen with shields, the bulk of the royal armies.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5 (era-typical). Evidence: iron and steel weapons are coded present (Seshat https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/208); little body armour

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: professional soldiers coded present from 320 CE (Seshat https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/208) alongside clan levies

count.note: Educated guess. Javelin men and skirmishers.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5 minus. Evidence: self bows

count.note: Educated guess. A few horsemen; the highland armies fought on foot.

Educated guess. Red Sea craft from Adulis; the kingdom had a strong navy for trade between Nubia, Yemen and India (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Aksum), with no ship count before the 525 Himyar expedition.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: sewn-plank Red Sea ships, not war galleys

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.5. Evidence: multi-column campaigns; in RIE 189 Ezana led the main division for 23 days while detachments raided the countryside (Hatke 2013, p. 113, https://dlib.nyu.edu/awdl/isaw/hatke2013-aksum-and-nubia/)

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.5. Evidence: royal armies with named units plus clan levies; provinces ruled indirectly through tributary rulers (Seshat https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/208)

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.5-0.75. Evidence: recent victories over the Beja and the Noba recorded on Ezana's inscriptions

weapons.note: Anchor 3 (iron weapons) minus. Evidence: iron and steel coded present (Seshat https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/208); spears, swords, bows; no torsion artillery.

armor.note: Anchor 2 (bronze scale) to 3. Evidence: shields, little metal body armour recorded.

ships.note: Anchor 2. Evidence: sewn-plank Red Sea trading ships, no oared war galleys.

fortification.note: Anchor 2. Evidence: stone palaces and elite buildings at Aksum; no city walls of the Mediterranean kind.

logistics.note: Anchor 2. Evidence: Ousanas built a road to bring tribute and provisions to his troops (RIE 186, Hatke 2013 p. 32); pack animals and porters.

communications.note: Anchor 2 (couriers). Evidence: royal couriers; no relay system recorded.

gdpPerCapita.note: No Maddison value for the Horn of Africa before 1950. Maddison 2023 (OWID grapher CSV, https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true) has Egypt 1,116 (1 CE) and 1,164 (730); highland Aksum with its Red Sea trade is placed below Egypt and near the 700 of the mali-empire-1330 snapshot.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Tribute and Red Sea trade revenue paid the royal armies; no budget survives.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Gold, silver and bronze coinage (from c. 270, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Aksum), ironwork, stone quarrying for stelae.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Plough farming with terraces, dams and irrigation (teff, wheat, barley; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Aksum).

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in a pre-modern age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model as the classical and medieval snapshots.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. Royal roads such as the one Ousanas built for supplies (RIE 186); caravan routes Aksum-Adulis.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. Adulis, the principal Red Sea port (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Aksum).

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Red Sea trading craft; no figures.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Foot armies with pack animals in broken highland country.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. Cattle, donkeys and mules; one campaign alone took 10,560 cattle (RIE 189).

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2 (familiar terrain, local supply, population support) to 1.3: a highland plateau behind escarpments and lowland heat an invader is not adapted to.

notes: Snapshot = 350, Ezana (r. c. 320s-360) after the Beja campaign and his conversion to Christianity, before the Nubian campaign that Hatke dates to 360. No army size survives from any Aksumite source: every force count is an educated guess sized against the inscriptions' casualty and spoil tallies (RIE 189, RIE 185), so the force mix and active personnel are the weakest values. Population and area are Seshat codings (Axum I and II). Border: world_300 Axum is the file at or before the year; it covers only the highland core (89,000 km2), while areaKm2 is researched. Population convention: the Ethiopian-Eritrean kingdom; claimed South Arabian and Nubian lands (in Ezana's titles) are not counted. No elephants are counted: none appear in the 4th-century records used here.
